name: returns an exactly valid expression when one exists
input: three targets, including repeated input values
test:
import ast

def assert_expression(values, target):
    expression = build_expression(values, target)
    assert isinstance(expression, str) and expression
    tree = ast.parse(expression, mode='eval')
    literals = []

    def evaluate(node):
        if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, int) and not isinstance(node.value, bool):
            literals.append(node.value)
            return node.value
        if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp) and type(node.op) in (ast.Add, ast.Sub, ast.Mult):
            left = evaluate(node.left)
            right = evaluate(node.right)
            if isinstance(node.op, ast.Add):
                return left + right
            if isinstance(node.op, ast.Sub):
                return left - right
            return left * right
        raise AssertionError('expression uses an unsupported token')

    assert evaluate(tree.body) == target
    assert sorted(literals) == sorted(values)

assert_expression([3, 4, 8], 20)
assert_expression([5, 5, 1], 20)
assert_expression([0, 2, 3], 6)

name: reports an impossible target without adding forbidden operations
input: three integers that cannot reach the requested target with plus, minus, and multiply

name: requires all inputs rather than a convenient subset
input: a target equal to one input but three values supplied
test:
import ast
expression = build_expression([1, 2, 6], 6)
assert isinstance(expression, str)
tree = ast.parse(expression, mode='eval')
values = [node.value for node in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(node, ast.Constant)]
assert sorted(values) == [1, 2, 6]
